displayQuote: The Architect Can Only Advise His Client to Plant Vines

meta.title: Who really said "The Architect Can Only Advise His Client to Plant Vines"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Herbert Hoover. Frank Lloyd Wright wrote it in his 1931 lecture “To the Young Man in Architecture”; Hoover’s similar line is about engineers.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Architect Can Only Advise His Client to Plant Vines'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is Frank Lloyd Wright’s, from a lecture printed in 1931. Hoover used the same joke — pointed at architects, in praise of engineers.

answer.label: Not Herbert Hoover — actually Frank Lloyd Wright
answer.sourceLine: Wright wrote it as point 11 of the fourteen instructions that close his lecture “To the Young Man in Architecture,” printed in Two Lectures on Architecture (The Art Institute of Chicago, 1931): “The physician can bury his mistakes,—but the architect can only advise his client to plant vines.” Herbert Hoover did write a near-identical joke, but in his version the architects are the ones getting away with something — his subject is the engineer, who cannot.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

source.excerpt: 11. Then go as far away as possible from home to build your first buildings. The physician can bury his mistakes,—but the architect can only advise his client to plant vines.
trail: 1913 — the shape of the joke already exists. A New York Evening Post gardening column by Walter B. Hayward argues that architects’ mistakes “have to be right out in plain sight, unless they can be hidden by vines and trees” — a precursor located by lexicographer Barry Popik and printed by Quote Investigator ↗.

1931 — Frank Lloyd Wright closes his lecture “To the Young Man in Architecture” with fourteen numbered points, and number eleven carries the line in its original form. It is printed in Two Lectures on Architecture (The Art Institute of Chicago, 1931 ↗), page 62 according to Quote Investigator ↗.

1950s — Herbert Hoover builds the same joke into his set piece on engineering, aimed the other way: the engineer “cannot, like the architects, cover his failures with trees and vines” (Hoover Presidential Foundation ↗, which dates its text to an Engineer’s Week article of 1954). Quote Investigator cites a version from Hoover’s 9 February 1950 address to the Engineering Society of the Moles.

1953–54 — Wright uses the jest again in the New York Times Magazine of 4 October 1953, the version Wikiquote ↗ and the standard quotation dictionaries carry. A year later a Cleveland newspaper printed the swap that stuck — “doctor” for “physician” — crediting Reader’s Digest.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator from the 1931 volume, page 62. The lecture ends with fourteen numbered instructions to young architects; the vines gag is the tail of number eleven, whose real advice is to build your first buildings a long way from home.

author.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.bio: Frank Lloyd Wright was the most famous American architect of the twentieth century — the Prairie houses, Fallingwater, the spiral of the Guggenheim — and, by the 1930s, an equally practised writer and lecturer. The vines line comes from that second career: a printed lecture aimed squarely at young architects, in which the joke is the sugar on a set of unsentimental instructions about preparation and humility. He kept using it for the rest of his life, and it reached most people through a New York Times Magazine piece published in 1953.

Not Herbert Hoover, whose similar line is about engineers, not architects.

misattribution.heading: Why Hoover gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually honest mix-up: Herbert Hoover really did write a sentence about architects hiding their failures behind greenery. It is just not this sentence, and in his version the architect is the villain of the piece rather than the speaker.

items.tag: Right joke, wrong side of it
items.why: Hoover — a mining engineer long before he was a president — built a famous set piece contrasting the engineer with every other profession. The engineer, he wrote, “cannot bury his mistakes in the grave like the doctors… He cannot, like the architects, cover his failures with trees and vines” (Hoover Presidential Foundation ↗). The architects are his foil. He is not advising anyone to plant anything.

items.scope: The date, when Hoover is credited
items.why: Quote Investigator dates a Hoover version to his address of 9 February 1950 to the Engineering Society of the Moles in New York, published in Addresses Upon the American Road: 1948–1950; the Hoover Presidential Foundation dates its own text to a 1954 Engineer’s Week article; Wikiquote prints it from chapter 11 of his memoirs. All of those come after Wright’s 1931 lecture ↗.

Wright wrote “physician,” not “doctor.” Quote Investigator finds the “doctor” substitution in print in a Cleveland newspaper in 1954, credited to Reader’s Digest — and that softened version is the one that circulates today, usually with no source attached at all ↗.

items.scope: The doctors half of the joke
items.why: A 1941 newspaper column relaying an item from the March Ladies’ Home Journal has the radio writer Arch Oboler tell Wright that doctors can bury their mistakes but a wrong house is a living reproach; Wright answers that architects “get the client to plant vines” (Quote Investigator ↗). Oboler fed the line; he did not coin it, and Wright had already printed it a decade earlier.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Frank Lloyd Wright’s, from a lecture printed in 1931. Herbert Hoover later used the same joke and aimed it the other way — at architects, in defence of engineers (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The joke lands because it flatters the profession it insults. A physician’s failures are private; an architect’s stand in the street for a century, and the only remedy on offer is greenery. Wright did not deliver it as a standalone epigram — he buried it at the end of a scolding instruction to young architects to spend ten years preparing and then build their first buildings as far from home as possible, precisely because they would not be able to hide them.

Herbert Hoover liked the same joke well enough to rebuild it from the engineer’s side, where the architect becomes the lucky one who gets to plant ivy over his errors. That inversion is the likeliest reason his name migrated onto Wright’s wording: two of the most-quoted Americans of the century, one professional grudge, one shared punchline about vines.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator credits lexicographer Barry Popik with finding the joke already fully formed in 1913, in a New York Evening Post gardening column by Walter B. Hayward: architects’ mistakes, he wrote, “have to be right out in plain sight, unless they can be hidden by vines and trees.” The columns were collected the following year as The Commuter’s Garden (Quote Investigator ↗).

The older half of the gag — that doctors get to bury their errors — is older still. Quote Investigator prints an 1883 Michigan agricultural lecture using it against farmers: the farmer’s mistakes “remain above ground where they are seen and known by all men.” Wright’s contribution was the vines, and the compression.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the line to Frank Lloyd Wright's 1931 lecture "To the Young Man in Architecture" (point 11, Two Lectures on Architecture, Art Institute of Chicago, page 62), and documents a 1913 Walter B. Hayward precursor found by Barry Popik, an 1883 farming version of the doctors-bury-their-mistakes gag, a 1941 Arch Oboler exchange, Herbert Hoover's 1950 Engineering Society of the Moles version, the 1953 New York Times rewording, and a 1954 Cleveland Plain Dealer printing of the "doctor" variant credited to Reader's Digest.

Wikiquote lists "The physician can bury his mistakes, but the architect can only advise his clients to plant vines" in Frank Lloyd Wright's sourced Quotes section, cited to New York Times Magazine (4 October 1953), and notes the paraphrase beginning "A doctor can bury his mistakes".

Wikiquote prints Herbert Hoover's engineering passage containing "He cannot, like the architects, cover his failures with trees and vines", placed under The Memoirs of Herbert Hoover and marked as excerpted from Chapter 11, "The Profession of Engineering".

The Hoover Presidential Foundation publishes Hoover's text "Engineering as a Profession", labelled an article in Engineer's Week and dated 1954, containing "He cannot bury his mistakes in the grave like the doctors" and "He cannot, like the architects, cover his failures with trees and vines."
HathiTrust's catalog record shows Two Lectures on Architecture with publication date 1931, and its scanned copy is restricted to limited, search-only access rather than full view.
HathiTrust's catalog record shows The Commuter's Garden published 1914 and available in full view (public domain).
Frank Lloyd Wright was born 8 June 1867 and died 9 April 1959, and is described as an American architect, designer, writer and educator.
The Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation states that it owns numerous copyrighted materials of Frank Lloyd Wright's, along with trademarks and rights of publicity, and reserves all rights in them.
